introduction-the-hard-drive-in-the-cloud.core: EBS provides network-attached block volumes for EC2: persistent disks that survive instance stops, live in one AZ, replicate within that AZ, and can be resized, snapshotted and changed in type online. Unlike instance store, data persists independently of the instance.

first_principles.problem: An engineer stores database files on instance store and loses them when the instance stops.
truths: Block storage needs low latency, so it lives in one AZ.
Network-attached volumes can move between instances.
derivation: Remember **AZ scope**: volumes attach only within their AZ.

analogy.title: An external hard drive you can plug into any computer in the room
analogy.story: Unplug it, and your data's still there.
analogy.breaks: Hard drives can move between rooms; EBS needs a snapshot to change AZ.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: More space without stopping the app.

code.text:
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-123 --size 500
# then inside the instance:
sudo growpart /dev/nvme1n1 1 && sudo xfs_growfs /data

check.q: Can you attach an EBS volume to an instance in another AZ?
check.a: No; create a snapshot and restore it in the target AZ.

volume-types-the-performance-matrix.core: EBS types: gp3 (general SSD, 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s baseline, independently provisionable), io2 Block Express (high, consistent IOPS up to 256k, sub-ms latency, 99.999% durability), st1 (throughput HDD for big sequential reads) and sc1 (cold HDD). Instance-level EBS bandwidth limits also apply.

first_principles.problem: A database on gp2 hits IOPS limits tied to volume size, and the team overprovisions terabytes to get IOPS.

analogy.title: Choosing roads
analogy.story: A good dual carriageway for most traffic (gp3), a dedicated racetrack (io2) and wide freight roads for slow heavy loads (st1).
analogy.breaks: Roads don't have per-car speed limits tied to the vehicle; instance bandwidth caps EBS speed.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Smaller volume, needed IOPS, lower bill.

check.q: What's the key advantage of gp3 over gp2?
check.a: IOPS and throughput can be provisioned independently of volume size, at a lower base price.

multi-attach-clustering-in-the-cloud.core: io1/io2 volumes support Multi-Attach: one volume attached to up to 16 Nitro instances in the same AZ. EBS doesn't coordinate writes, so applications must use a cluster-aware filesystem (GFS2, OCFS2) or application-level fencing. Standard filesystems like ext4 or XFS will corrupt.

first_principles.problem: Two instances mount the same XFS volume via Multi-Attach and corrupt it within minutes.
truths: Normal filesystems assume a single writer.
derivation: Use a **cluster-aware filesystem** or app-managed I/O fencing.
Prefer **EFS/FSx** when you just need shared files.

analogy.title: Several people writing in one notebook at once
analogy.story: Without strict turn-taking, the pages become nonsense.
analogy.breaks: People can see each other writing; instances can't see each other's cached writes.

example.title: Choosing shared storage
flow: Need: Oracle RAC-style cluster → io2 Multi-Attach + cluster FS

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Multi-Attach is for cluster-aware software only.

check.q: Why can't you use XFS with Multi-Attach?
check.a: XFS assumes a single writer; concurrent writers corrupt its metadata.

snapshots-data-lifecycle-manager-dlm.core: EBS snapshots are incremental, point-in-time backups stored in S3-backed storage: only changed blocks are saved, but each snapshot restores a full volume. Data Lifecycle Manager automates creation, retention, cross-region copies and archiving on schedules by tag. Restores lazy-load unless Fast Snapshot Restore is enabled.

first_principles.problem: Manual snapshots are forgotten, and restored volumes are slow at first.
truths: Restored volumes fetch blocks on first read.

analogy.title: Saving only the changes in a document's version history
analogy.story: Each version can be opened in full, but storage holds only the edits.
analogy.breaks: Opening a document version is instant; restored volumes lazy-load blocks unless pre-warmed.

check.q: Why might a volume restored from a snapshot be slow initially?
check.a: Blocks are lazily loaded from snapshot storage on first access unless Fast Snapshot Restore is enabled.
